comments.author: secabeen
comments.textRawHtml:
The tech sector is the most software-defined and virtual of all sectors, it's natural that they are first to change. Other industries need to make capital investments to adapt to change.

You can see a similar history with electrification. A few industries went quickly, but then it took like a decade of little growth before the true benefits showed up. As an example, take a factory that was built around hyrdo-power like a grain mill. You can't just take an electric motor and drop it in in place of the water wheel. It doesn't fit, the wheel is outside, there isn't room between the mill and the wall, etc. Only when you completely rebuild a new mill building designed around the features and limitations of the electric motor do you see the major benefits.

Same thing here; it will be new factories and new companies that are designed from the ground up around AI and its benefits and limitations that really move the needle.

children.author: Zigurd
children.textRawHtml:
Cool analogy, but there's another possibility: software is uniquely suited for being boosted by LLM-based coding agents. That's not to say LLMs are useless in other domains, but they may not yield as much benefit.

Software creation tools have been worked on for decades to keep fallible human coders out of trouble as much as possible. Starting with compilers that enforce or at least encourage coding style humans can understand. Compilers embody formal definitions of language syntax. Lint and other static analysis technologies contribute by identifying problematic patterns in code. Leak detectors identify memory management problems. Profilers identify performance problems.

Few other endeavors have this much tooling that serendipitously happens to help help LLM-based agents be more useful and less error prone.

A lot of discussion around AI is very high-level and abstract. It helps to dig in and identify the characteristics that actually make a domain more or less amenable to being boosted by AI.

children.author: rwyinuse
children.textRawHtml:
I think LLM's will prove to be useful in any domain where most work happens in front of a computer. As LLM's make programming cheap, they also reduce the cost of building new software that automates work currently performed by humans in other fields.

If you provide best models with all the data and context an average white collar worker has to perform their job, in most cases they will do just fine. But in real world that context is often scattered over multiple systems, or sometimes exists only in people's heads. I believe that's the main bottleneck for adoption now.

children.author: eslaught
children.textRawHtml:
You're missing the biggest suggestion from the GP's post: that the key to LLM success is verifiability.

Software has high verifiability through compilers, linters, static analysis, leak/memory corruption detection tools, or the very least, running the program to see if it crashes.

Math (as has been making the headlines recently) has high verifiability through automated theorem provers. Notably some of the non-mechanized math results from LLMs have been demonstrated to be wrong (and presumably many more are being checked; these aren't exactly easy to understand proofs).

Game playing (chess, go, Star Craft, etc.) is similarly verifiable: you get your score and you always know how you did in the end (even if not in the moment).

Making assumptions about LLMs in non-veriable domains is making a claim about LLMs that doesn't match their current capabilities. Maybe they'll get there and maybe they won't; I can speculate as well as you can but we're both guessing, so I'm not sure how much value the speculation has.

children.author: david_shi
children.textRawHtml:
I think we'll naturally develop intuition and infrastructure for fault-tolerant ways to implement LLMs in non-verifiable domains, i.e. requiring multiple, independent agents agree on a direction from multiple angles before taking an action.

But we're definitely very early on this trend.

That's not to say it isn't useful, and if youre on top of it you can guide it away from doing that.

children.author: bunderbunder
children.textRawHtml:
This assumes that a significant portion of the average white collar worker’s job is amenable to automation.

But most white collar workers I know spend most their time either talking to each other, or thinking real hard about what to say the next time they get together to talk. If that’s generally true then it would suggest that there isn’t much white collar work that LLMs, which are now widely regarded as exceptionally poor communicators, can do particularly well.

children.author: pj_mukh
children.textRawHtml:
I think the bear case (see:short term) benefit is that any and all information gathering, management and parsing the employee did between organizing with other employees will be automated, allowing the employee to do more organizing over the same unit of time.

The bull case (see: long term) is that the “organizing and talking” as long as it’s not something that is essentially human (like caretaking, nursing etc.) will happen between personal agents of sorts with only the deeper judgments being left to the humans opening up even more increases in productivity. This is already happening with PR reviews in a lot of workplaces.

Though I’m guessing most workplaces outside of tech will require total reorganization around this reality, but more likely this way of running will mean newer upstarts challenging incumbents refusing to change as it’s always been.

children.author: alfjal
children.textRawHtml:
They certainly can, but I wonder if the cost will be deskilling your employees and leading brainstorming sessions towards AI psychosis.

I've seen much time wasted on strange ideas originated by an LLM. It's a lot easier for a human to organically have good ideas than to refute LLM-generated ideas that are a dead end.

children.author: epihelix
children.textRawHtml:
If people are in charge of project management, and repeatedly fail to recognise poor ideas and instead pursue them to the detriment of productivity, then they probably shouldn't be managing that project.

All AI is doing here is rapidly identifying the people who have Peter-principled themselves.

> It's a lot easier for a human to organically have good ideas than to refute LLM-generated ideas that are a dead end.

What works better is when you can use an LLM to obtain a negative opinion on your own ideas that you think are good. LLMs aren't great at original thinking, but they're pretty good at finding the flaws in poorly thought-through human ideas.
